newsitem.title: UZBEKISTAN: Uzbek chief urges press freedom, few believe him.
newsitem.headline: Uzbek chief urges press freedom, few believe him.

text.p: Uzbekistan's state press on Saturday published a call by President Islam Karimov for greater freedom of information but few believe it signals an end to tight media curbs in the former Soviet republic.

Karimov, a former communist party chief, said in an interview that stronger democratic institutions and greater protection of human rights should be guaranteed in the central Asian republic, which he runs with an iron grip.
"Promoting a democratic press will be the third direction of political reform," he said.
The moon and stars have replaced the communist era hammer and sickle on the Uzbek flag but little else has changed in the country since independence in 1991.
The front pages of dailies like Narodnoye Slovo (People's Word) regularly place photographs of Karimov and publish his long unabridged speeches.
A typical story in Saturday's edition of Pravda Vostoka (Truth of the East) featured a brigade of heroic tractor drivers who ploughed land for next year's cotton crop in record time.
Liberal Russian newspapers are banned in the resource-rich and largely desert nation of 23 million people.
Printed criticism of the government can only be found in copies of underground opposition newspapers smuggled in from Russia.
State television has even stopped broadcasting the Uzbek currency's official exchange rate and even the most commonplace economic indicators are classified.
"The government will tell you there are no censors," said a foreign diplomat who has to trawl daily through the Uzbek press for hints of policy changes. "But of course there are."
Asked by a Western reporter on Friday to comment on press censorship in Uzbekistan, Karimov replied disarmingly: "I can accept we are not at your level but we are trying to improve."
He even offered the reporter a job with an Uzbek newspaper saying: "We need your help."
Last week the republic's obedient parliament approved the first reading of a new law on press and information.
Few details are known of the new law which is yet to be published but observers say it is expected to contain guidelines for the protection of journalists.
However observers warn that all is not what it seems in the looking-glass world of Uzbek politics.
"Guidelines to criticise mean the government is about to give the nod to journalists on who exactly they will be allowed to criticise," a Western observer said.
He said "protection" for reporters was more likely to mean Soviet-style guarantees of a steady job while he feared a new "standards committee" could be used to legitimise censorship.
It was not clear from Karimov's speech how far he intended to relax controls on the media.
A truck driver clicked his tongue in disapproval at the newspapers on sale in the Uzbek captial Tashkent. "They want to paint a nice picture for everyone but it is fake," he said.
